# Hidden triggers and ordinary-use policies pose different audit problems {#sec-threats}

A reviewer may know the published attack and audit methods; the attacker may
know them too. The reviewer's random choices remain private until the artifact
or transcript under examination is fixed. An **output-only reviewer** can
submit inputs and inspect responses. A **weights-access reviewer** can also
inspect and execute the supplied model, record activations, and intervene on
its computation. A third setting supplies a committed training trajectory.
These settings concern the evidence available, not the reviewer's competence.
An API audit additionally needs assurance that the tested system is the one
deployed; a weight audit needs the same assurance about the surrounding tools,
memory, and serving code.

## An attacker supplies a rare activation input

Draguns et al. construct transformer backdoors whose activating inputs are
computationally difficult to discover even with weight access
[@draguns2025unelicitable]. Their cryptographic construction is intended to
withhold the hidden output behavior until the appropriate input is supplied.
It distinguishes **unelicitability**, difficulty finding an activating input,
from **undetectability**, difficulty recognizing that the artifact is suspect.
The authors explicitly stop short of full white-box undetectability against a
representative distribution of normally trained language models.

In a deployment scenario, an attacker might supply an activating input through
a retrieved document. A tool-using system could then act on the changed output,
but communication with a controller and persistence across cleared contexts
require additional system mechanisms. These are threat-model extensions, not
results established by that paper. The backdoor need not recognize an auditor:
its activation can be rare in testing and deliberately arranged in deployment.
This does not establish covert behavior on a broad semantic class of ordinary
customer requests.

## Boosting and topic-specific lying must operate on useful inputs

A sponsor-serving policy acts on naturally occurring recommendation situations.
A topic-specific lying policy likewise answers incorrectly on a semantic class,
such as factual questions about a particular organization, while preserving
other answers. For binary tasks it has the same abstract form
$g(x)=f(x)\oplus t(x)$, now with a semantic predicate $t$. The cost of recognizing
that predicate is not the $k-1$ raw-bit conjunction cost in Proposition 1.

Continued training can change such policies without adding layers. AuditBench
provides concrete trained examples of hidden behaviors and resistance to
confession; audit success varies with training method and available tools
[@sheshadri2026auditbench]. ROME separately demonstrates selective factual
editing within existing transformer MLP weights [@meng2023rome]. These results
support architecture-preserving behavioral change. They do not prove that an
arbitrary policy can be inserted into an efficiency-optimal model at negligible
cost, or that the resulting change defeats a competent audit.

The legitimate capabilities may also support recognizing evaluation contexts.
Consequently, an additional review-avoidance policy need not require additional
stored parameters. Its opportunity cost in capability, inference work, or
description length remains a separate question. Matching layer structure and
parameter count eliminates one conspicuous difference; it does not establish
statistical or computational indistinguishability of weights.

## Weight access adds evidence without making interpretation exhaustive

A known clean parent checkpoint gives the reviewer a weight difference to
investigate. An independently trained model of comparable capability instead
provides a behavioral control; its weights need not align coordinate by
coordinate. Neither comparison labels every discrepancy as malicious.

The interpretability literature supplies both instruments and limits.
Hase et al. find that causal-tracing localization does not generally predict
where factual editing succeeds [@hase2023localization]. Thus finding an edit
that changes an answer does not establish the location or complete meaning of
the original computation. Conversely, Marks et al. report that three of four
auditing teams recovered a deliberately hidden objective using combinations
of behavioral methods, interpretability, and training-data analysis
[@marks2025auditing]. AuditBench also finds that adding white-box tools need
not improve a particular investigator agent's performance
[@sheshadri2026auditbench]. These are findings about specified auditing
procedures, not a general ordering of all possible reviewers: a reviewer with
more access can always choose to use only the output-only procedure.

Goldwasser et al. establish a stronger theoretical obstruction for particular
random-feature model families: under cryptographic assumptions, efficient
reviewers cannot distinguish distributions of clean and backdoored models
even with full descriptions and training data [@goldwasser2024backdoors].
This quantifies over informed reviewers, not merely reviewers unaware of the
construction. It neither covers every transformer nor bounds the cost of
frequent, ordinary-use boosting. A sequence of attacks and countermeasures
does not by itself prove that concealment is always possible.

Recent extensions strengthen particular white-box results without settling
this deployment question. Choudhary et al. study image classifiers, including
vision transformers, with indistinguishability relative to a specified
randomized reference distribution [@choudhary2026sparse]. Bogdanov, Rosen, and
Vafa give statistical white-box indistinguishability for a class of feedforward
networks, with the hidden advantage being access to particular adversarial
examples [@bogdanov2026statistical]. Neither result, as stated, establishes
frequent covert recommendation bias in an efficiency-optimal language model.
